wonton.e: Borrowed from Cantonese 雲吞 /云吞 (wan⁴ tan¹, wan⁴ tan⁴).
wonton.x: The wonton will be done when the crab filling is cooked through and the wonton are very soft.

woodchuck.e: Folk-etymological adaption of Cree ocêk, otchek (“fisher”), Ojibwe ojiig (“fisher, marten”), or a similar term in a related Algonquian language, subsequently reapplied to…

woodcock.x: If I loved you not, I would laugh at you, and see you / Run your neck into the noose, and cry, "A woodcock!"

wooded.e: From Middle English woded (“concealed by trees”), equivalent to wood + -ed.
wooded.x: Through the thickly wooded and precipitous slopes on either side of the line there are one or two short rock tunnels.

woodpecker.x: On its summit towered aloft the fir tree which has often been referred to, like a mighty mast, full of woodpeckers' holes.

woodruff.e: From Old English wudurofe, from wudu (“wood”) + rofe, of uncertain meaning and origin.

woodwork.e: From Middle English woodewerk (“carpentry”), equivalent to wood + work.
woodwork.x: Some woodwork and the plaster ceiling medallions have been duplicated to match the originals.

woolen.e: From Middle English wollen, wullen, from Old English wyllen, from Proto-Germanic *wullīnaz (“woollen”), equivalent to wool + -en.
woolen.x: Woolen threads were an occult means, according to the Roman poet Horace, of depriving a person of virility.

woolly.e: From Middle English wolly, equivalent to wool + -y. Cognate with Saterland Frisian wullich (“woolly”), Dutch wollig (“woolly”), German wollig (“woolly”), Swedish ullig…
woolly.x: Put on a woolly jumper and turn down the thermostat.

wordplay.x: Even this modest wordplay was an outlier: Sagers counted only three backronyms across the ’70s and ’80s.

wordsmith.e: The noun is derived from word + smith (“craftsperson who works metal into desired forms; (by extension) one who makes anything”). The verb is derived from the noun.
wordsmith.x: She has always been known as a capable wordsmith, but in this latest novel she also shows surprising emotional depth.

workaholic.x: All workaholics should move to Hong Kong, where working hours average over 50 per week.

workday.e: From Middle English werkdai, werkedei, werkedai, from Old English weorcdæġ (“workday”), equivalent to work + day.
workday.x: It will take five workdays to process your application.

workforce.x: The rail sector's ageing workforce (28% of workers are over 50 years old) means that about 15,000 people could retire from the industry by 2025.

workhorse.e: From Middle English werkehorse, equivalent to work + horse.
workhorse.x: Those old machines are not very glamorous, but even 20 years after their introduction, they are still the workhorses of the industry.

workout.x: The following guidelines for smart weekly scheduling can simplify this piece of the planning: Swim three or four workouts each week.

worksheet.e: From work + sheet. First use appears c. 1823 in the publications of Isaac D'Israeli.

worktop.x: The cupboards were oak and the worktop was granite.

worldly.e: From Middle English worldly, worldlich, wordly (adjective), from Old English woruldlīċ, worldlīċ, weoroldlīċ (“worldly; earthly; temporal; mundane.

worldview.e: A calque of German Weltanschauung, equivalent to world + view.
worldview.x: According to the BfV, the JA promotes an ethno-nationalist worldview that ostracizes anyone who is not a native, white German.

worldwide.x: A large meteorite impact would cause worldwide extinction of life.

wormhole.e: First use appears c. 1594. From worm + hole. In the scientific sense, introduced by John Archibald Wheeler in 1957.
wormhole.x: Wormhole distortion has overloaded main power systems!

wormwood.e: From Middle English wormwode, a folk etymology (as if worm + wood) of wermode (“wormwood”), from Old English wermōd (“wormwood, absinthe”), from Proto-West Germanic…
wormwood.x: Cliff took two glasses and filled one with wine And one with wormwood.

worsen.e: From Middle English wursnen; equivalent to worse + -en.
worsen.x: Global warming has worsened the weather.

worshipper.e: Inherited from Middle English wirshiper, worchyppar, worscheper, worschepour, worschiper, worschippar, worshipore; equivalent to worship + -er.
worshipper.x: The temple was filled with worshippers.

worsted.e: Inherited from Middle English worstede, worsted, from Worstede (now Worstead; Old English *Wurϸestede), a town in Norfolk, England.
worsted.x: Finally he took a ball of worsted and tied strings of it across the back passage and across the opposite door.

worthwhile.x: Doing volunteer work to help others is truly worthwhile.

wraith.e: Borrowed from Middle Scots wraith, first attested in 1513 in a translation of the Aeneid. The word has no certain etymology.
wraith.x: We might indeed have been the wraiths of the departed dead upon the dead sea of that dying planet for all the sound or sign we made in passing.

wrangle.e: The verb is derived from Middle English wranglen, wrangle (“to contend with (someone) in a test of strength; (figuratively) to make misleading arguments to entrap”).
wrangle.x: I stood where land and sea wrangled ferociously over the overlap.

wrapper.e: From Middle English wrappere, equivalent to wrap + -er.
wrapper.x: He proved to be a remarkably efficient wrapper of parcels.

wreckage.x: Explorers have found the 153-year-old wreckage of the Bay State, one the earlier propeller-driven steamships to ply the waters of the Great Lakes.

wrench.e: From Middle English wrench, from Old English wrenċ, from Proto-Germanic *wrankiz, from Proto-Indo-European *wreng- (“to turn”). Compare German Rank (“plot, intrigue”).
wrench.x: With a wrench, which threw his victim back upon the bed as though hurled from a height, he turned and sprang at us.

wrestle.e: The verb is derived from Middle English wrestlen, wrastlen (“to engage in grappling combat or sport, struggle, wrestle; to twist and turn, squirm, wriggle, writhe.
wrestle.x: Have we not wrestled a turn before now?

wrestler.e: From Middle English wrastlere, equivalent to wrestle + -er.
wrestler.x: it isn't easy to avoid all the wrestler's holds.

wretch.e: From Middle English wrecche, from Old English wreċċa (“exile, outcast”), from Proto-Germanic *wrakjô (“exile, fugitive, warrior”), from Proto-Indo-European *wreg- (“to…
wretch.x: The poor wretch, who lay motionless a long time, just began to recover his senses as a stage-coach came by.

wretched.e: From Middle English wrecched (“(adjective) characterized by or suffering hardship or misfortune, miserable, unfortunate, unhappy; indigent, poor.
wretched.x: I felt wretched after my wife died.

wriggle.e: From wrig + -le (frequentative suffix). Compare Dutch wriggelen (“to wriggle, squirm”), Low German wriggeln (“to wriggle”).
wriggle.x: Teachers often lose their patience when children wriggle in their seats.

wring.e: From Middle English wring, wringe, wringen, wryng, wrynge, wryngen, wryngyn, from Old English wringan (“to wring”), from Proto-Germanic *wringaną (“to squeeze, twist…
wring.x: Put the berries into a cheesecloth and wring the juice into a bowl.

wrinkle.e: From Middle English wrinkle, wrynkel (“crease, fold, wrinkle”), from the verb (see below). Cognate with Dutch wrinkel (“wrinkle, crease”).
wrinkle.x: Spending time out in the sun may cause you to develop wrinkles sooner.

wrongdoer.x: Get and keep wrongdoers out of your thorp (village).

wrongly.e: From Middle English wrongly, wrongliche, equivalent to wrong + -ly.
wrongly.x: I wrongly assumed that it would be an easy job.

wushu.e: From Mandarin 武術／武术 (wǔshù, “martial techniques”).

wyvern.e: Alteration of Middle English wyver (“viper”), from Old Northern French wivre, from Vulgar Latin *vivra, *vibra, from Latin vīpera (“viper; snake, serpent”).
wyvern.x: Above the shield was the well-known Midland crest of a legless wyvern (a wyvern normally has two legs).
